item.content:encoded:
Brandon Valenzuela began the 2026 season as catching depth, but when the season was over he had seemingly solidified himself as the backup catcher for the foreseeable future for the Toronto Blue Jays. What looked like a temporary promotion after Alejandro Kirk fractured his left thumb became a season-long audition in which Valenzuela established himself as an elite defender. He even earned recognition as an American League Gold Glove finalist.
That depth is valuable, but it also brings up a legitimate offseason question. With Kirk entrenched as the starter, would the Blue Jays be better served keeping Valenzuela as a high-end backup or using his rising value to address a more pressing need elsewhere on the roster?
Why Valenzuela has real trade value
Valenzuela’s market starts with his defense. In 91 games as a rookie, he ranked among the top five major-league catchers in Statcast Fielding Run Value and FanGraphs’ defensive rating. His framing and blocking gave Toronto’s pitchers a steady target, while his arm helped him throw out 19 of 63 attempted base stealers.
He also held his own at the plate for the first half of the season when he produced a .241/.322/.407 line and a 106 wRC+. Valenzuela’s age and years of club control would certainly be intriguing for prospective teams. Getting a 26-year-old catcher who has already shown he can handle a major-league staff is the type of profile that could be the centre of a decent trade package.
However, there will be detractors around the league. While Valenzuela finished with nine home runs, a double-digit walk rate and a .688 OPS across 271 plate appearances, his second half numbers were not good. He produced a .182/.276/.299 with a 65 wRC+ after the All-Star break. His walk rate held steady, but the strikeouts started to tick up and and he hit just two home runs.
To be fair, rookie catchers often wear down under the physical and mental demands of the position, and teams will likely value his defence first. But it does, limit the return Toronto can reasonably expect. Valenzuela alone is unlikely to fetch an established middle-of-the-order bat or a frontline starter. A more realistic outcome would be a need-for-need deal involving a player with similar control and upside.
What could the Blue Jays get on the trade market for Brandon Valenzuela?
There are several teams that are likely looking for a catcher this offseason and the free agent market is somewhat thin. Three teams that could meet a need-for-need trade are the New York Yankees, Chicago Cubs and Cincinnati Reds.
Yankees - Luis Garcia Jr.
The most ambitious idea would be a deal with the Yankees centred on Luis García Jr. García hit 30 home runs with an .830 OPS in 2026, although his production slipped to a .264/.302/.434 slash line after New York acquired him at the deadline but they are already rumored to be shopping around Garcia this offseason.
His left-handed power would interest Toronto, and returning Garcia back to second base while filling in for Guerrero Jr. at first could address the need to get more pop from the right side of the infield.
The Yankees would almost certainly demand more than Valenzuela in return. But they are also desperate to upgrade on Austin Wells behind the dish and they will need to potentially replace other players such as Trent Grisham, Jazz Chisholm, David Bednar, and Paul Goldschmidt just to name a few.
Cubs - Kevin Alcántara
Chicago is potentially losing Carson Kelly behind the plate, putting the Cubs in need of a replacement. Kevin Alcántara is a 24-year-old right-handed outfielder that will be fighting for playing time with the South Siders. Alcántara hit 20 home runs with an .852 OPS at Triple-A in 2026.
The power and handedness should intrigue Toronto who currently only has two MLB outfielders who bat from the right side and that's Anthony Santander (a switch-hitter and outfielder is a loose term with him) and Davis Schenider (who could be a non-tender candidate).
It could be risky to move a proven MLB backup catcher (at worst) in Valenzuela for Alcántara who has yet to stick around in the big leagues after 37 games over three stints dating back to 2024. But the Blue Jays need some flexibility in their outfield corps and after the Blue Jays had so much success with their last trade with the Cubs they might be wise to go to the well again.
Reds - JJ Bleday
JJ Bleday represents another version of the same need-for-need framework. The Cincinnati outfielder hit .217/.324/.416 with 24 home runs and 72 walks in 2026. Again, the pop is the selling point here and he's under team control through 2028.
His significant second-half drop and stronger production against right-handed pitching make him more of a platoon-oriented corner bat and, as stated, the Blue Jays already have a few of those in Nathan Lukes, Addison Barger, Sean Keys and Yohendrick Piñango. Still, if Cincinnati decides it needs a defensive upgrade behind the plate, Valenzuela could form the foundation of a conversation.
Keeping Valenzuela may still be the better move
The strongest argument against a trade is Kirk’s 2026 injury. Toronto learned how quickly catching depth can derail a season. Valenzuela helped stabilize a key piece of the Blue Jays roster and held his own.
There is also room for both catchers. Kirk is the clear starter, but carrying Valenzuela would allow Toronto to protect him from overuse and they could use either catcher at designated hitter on occasion
Valenzuela has enough value that the Blue Jays should not make him untouchable, and if another club is willing to exchange a controllable everyday outfielder, or a credible second-base option, Toronto would be justified in using its catching depth to improve a thinner area of the roster.
But dealing him simply because Kirk is ahead of him would be a mistake. Valenzuela’s defence, affordability and ability to step into a larger role give the Blue Jays more certainty than most teams possess behind their starting catcher. Unless the return clearly improves the 2027 roster, keeping one of baseball’s better defensive catching tandems is the safer—and probably smarter—choice.

Baseball Reference has him at a 1.1 WAR (down from 4.0). FanGraphs 3.1 (down from 4.1), giving him a value of $25.1 million to the Jays and Cubs.
He had a 3.3.74 FIP and a 3.58 xFIP, which is why the FanGraphs WAR is so much better than the Baseball Reference one.
Kevin's BABIP was .311 (up from.262 last year). 68.7% of his base runner were stranded (down from 72.2%).
His line drive rate was down a little bit (19.6% from 21.3 last year), ground ball rate up (40.3% down from 36.7), and fly ball rate much the same (40.3% from 42.0). 12.7% of fly balls hit off him left the park, up from 9.5.
His strikeout rate about the same (24.5% from 24.4), and his walk rate was down a bit (6.3% from 6.5).
Kevin's soft contact was up (17.4% from 15.1 last year) and hard contact about the same (35.9% from 36.2).
He was better against LHB (.251/.304/.389) than RHB (.269/.307/.459). He's been slightly better against LHB for his career.
He was better at home (3.83 ERA, batters hit .264/.299/.439) than on the road (5.40, .253/.313/.394).
Kevin was better in the first half of the season (4.33, .244/.296/.405) than the second half (4.82, .284/.320/.444).
Gausman by month:
- April: 7 starts, 2-2, 3.10. Batters hit .204/.244/.349, 5 home runs, 8 walks and 40 strikeouts.
- May: 5 starts, 2-1, 3.18. Batters hit .291/.316/.364, 1 home run, 4 walks and 26 strikeouts.
- June: 6 starts, 0-4, 6.47. Batters hit .262/.324/.556, 9 home runs, 12 walks and 34 strikeouts.
- July: 4 starts, 0-3, 6.10. Batters hit .280/.366/.317, 3 home runs, 11 walks and 23 strikeouts.
- August: 6 starts, 4-1, 4.54. Batters hit .275/.312/.443, 5 home runs, 8 walks and 33 strikeouts.
- September: 4 starts, 1-1, 4.43. Batters hit .267/.298/.478, 6 home runs, 4 walks and 28 strikeouts.
The Jays were 9-14 in his starts. The Cubs were 5-4 in his starts. Between the two teams, they averaged 4.05 runs scored in games he started. They scored 2 or less runs in 13 of his starts.
Days of rest:
- 4 days, 12 games: 3.54, .246/.288/.404.
- 5 days, 16 games: 5.26, .265/.313/.433.
- 6 or more days, 4 games: 4.50, .275/.326/.413
I love guys who are best on normal rest. I think we are all creatures of habit, you get in a routine and things go well, you leave that routine and they don't got as well. He was also best on normal rest last year.
Times through the order:
- 1st: Batters hit .233/.276/.346.
- 2nd: Batters hit .270/.318/.460.
- 3rd: Batters hit .286/.333/.478.
- And he faced 1 batter a fourth time, getting the out.
I wonder if he would consider being a reliever next year? That might be reading too much into one season, in 2025 he was pretty much the same for each of the first three times through the order.
By Catcher:
- Brandon Valenzuela: 4.46, .254/.298/.396 in 308 PA.
- Alejandro Kirk: 4.81, .263/.324/.419 in 185 PA.
- Carson Kelly: 4.20, .226/.268/.426 in 123 PA.
- Miguel Amaya: 5.75, .305/.333/.500 in 87 PA.
- Tyler Heineman: 2.31, .273/.319/.409 in 47 PA.
Kevin's best start, by GameScore, was a 78 on April 1st, at home against the Rockies. He went 6 innings, 2 hits, 0 earned runs, 0 walks, and 10 strikeouts. He also had a 77 and two 76s.
Worst start? A 13 in Chicago against the Cubs, on June 19th. You likely remember it: 2 innings, 7 hits, 7 earned runs, 1 home run, 4 walks and 3 strikeouts. We used six relievers, two days after a bullpen day, and the next day Patrick Corbin was pulled after 3.2 innings.
Kevin averaged 5.5 innings per start in his 23 starts with us. And about the same in his 9 starts with the Cubs. His one playoff start didn't go all that well: 3.1 innings, 3 earned.
He threw, for the most part, three pitches:
- Four Seamer: 93.8 mph (last year it averaged 94.5). Batters hit .289 against it (.230 last year).
- Split finger: 84 mph (last year it averaged 94.9). Batters hit .207 against it (.191 last year).
- Slider: 84.1 mph (last year it averaged 83.2). Batters hit .324 against it (.333 last year).
Random Baseball Savant numbers:
- Fastball Run Value: 87th percentile.
- Breaking Ball Run Value: 7th percentile.
- Chase Rate: 88th percentile.
- Strikeout %: 70th percentile.
- Walk %: 86th percentile.
- Barrell %: 46th percentile.
- Hard Hit %: 34th percentile.
- Expected ERA: 53rd percentile.
With the Jays, he posted a 53-51 record and a 3.63 ERA, with a 12.5 bWAR (and a 21 fWAR). FanGraphs says he was worth $167.6 million over his five-year contract, and he was paid $110 million, so we got more than our money's worth.
On the Jays career leaderboard:
- 11th in pitcher bWAR: 12.5.
- 7th in ERA: 3.62
- 11th in wins: 53 (tied with Jose Berrios)
- 11th in innings pitched: 861.0.
- 7th in strikeouts: 920.
- 9th in games started: 148.
He also started 7 playoff games (and pitched once in relief) for the Jays. He had a 3.79 ERA and a 2-4 record.
The last I saw, Gausman was talking about retirement, but he has said that he would consider coming back to the Jays. As I mentioned above, he was terrific the first time through the order, and far less good the second and third times. But I'm not sure that he would want to come back to pitch out of the pen.
The trade looks very good for the Jays, Brett Bateman was terrific for us, in his 41 games. Ty Southisene played well for 11 games with Vancouver, hitting .262/.380/.429. It will be interesting to watch how he does. FanGraphs had him listed as the Cubs 27th best prospect. He's fast and plays good defense in the middle of the infield.
It was great getting to watch Gausman pitch. The last five seasons wouldn't have been nearly as much fun without him.

Alejandro Kirk gave the Toronto Blue Jays a rare bright spot on an offense that struggled all season.
The catcher hit .278 with a .351 on-base percentage and a .415 slugging percentage. Kirk hit 10 home runs, drove in 43 runs and scored 26 times in 79 games. He collected 77 hits, including eight doubles and drew 33 walks against 38 strikeouts.
Injuries limited Kirk to 79 of Toronto’s 162 games. After a long season, Kirk is spending the offseason with his family.
He reposted photos from a Disney World trip on his Instagram story. The trip included his wife, Sofia Castañeda and their daughter, Emilia. The couple welcomed their daughter on Feb. 28, 2023.
Amid that news, what made headlines was trade chatter surrounding him.
Alejandro Kirk Labelled as a Trade Chip
Trade talk about Kirk surfaced Oct. 11. The Blue Bird Territory podcast posted a clip that day on X. The show features The Athletic’s Mitch Bannon, former Blue Jays outfielder Kevin Pillar and former pitcher Ricky Romero.
The post called Kirk “one of Toronto’s most VALUABLE trade chips.” In the clip, Pillar wondered about Kirk’s market value after injuries cost him much of the season. The clip spread online and some fans took it as a trade pitch.
Should Alejandro Kirk Be Traded?
The short answer is absolutely not. Bannon backed that view on X the same day. He wrote that he, Pillar and Romero all agreed Toronto should keep Kirk.
“This clip has gained some misguided traction, so to be clear, Kevin, Ricky and I all agreed the Jays shouldn’t trade Kirk,” he said. “We were more discussing why there’s been trade talk about him. In fact, I said he’s the exact mold of hitter the Jays covet, not a potential trade guy.”
The case against a trade starts with the contract. Toronto signed Kirk to a five-year, $58 million extension in March 2025. The deal covers 2026 through 2030 and averages $11.6 million per year.
Kirk also produces. His 114 wRC+ in 2026 topped his career mark of 111. He posted that mark despite missing more than two months. He walked in 10.5 percent of his plate appearances and struck out in 12.1 percent.
His defense adds to the case. In 2025, Kirk tied for third in MLB in fielding run value, with 21. He led all catchers in blocks above average and finished as a Gold Glove finalist.
Kirk also delivers in October. The two-time All-Star hit five home runs in the 2025 postseason. That ties the most by a catcher in one postseason. One was a go-ahead, three-run homer in World Series Game 3.
Toronto cannot afford to lose a productive bat. The Blue Jays’ offense was one of baseball’s worst this year. Trading a 27-year-old catcher on a long-term deal would deepen that problem.

Brandon Valenzuela, el hermosillense finalista por el Guante de Oro de MLB en su año de novato: ¿contra quién compite?
El receptor sonorense de los Blue Jays de Toronto figura entre los tres mejores defensivos de su posición en la Liga Americana. Conoce a sus rivales y la lista completa de los 60 finalistas.
El beisbol mexicano tendrá representación en la disputa por el reconocimiento defensivo más importante de las Grandes Ligas. El receptor hermosillense Brandon Valenzuela, de los Blue Jays de Toronto, fue anunciado este miércoles 14 de octubre como uno de los finalistas al Guante de Oro 2026, después de destacar detrás del plato durante su primera temporada en MLB.
El sonorense, de 26 años, competirá por el reconocimiento al mejor receptor defensivo de la Liga Americana contra Dillon Dingler, de los Tigres de Detroit, y Austin Wells, de los Yankees de Nueva York.
La empresa Rawlings presentó a los 60 finalistas, distribuidos en 10 categorías por cada liga, incluyendo la posición de jugador utility. Los ganadores serán anunciados el próximo domingo 1 de noviembre.
¿Por qué Brandon Valenzuela fue nominado al Guante de Oro 2026?
La nominación del hermosillense representa uno de los logros más importantes de su joven trayectoria, especialmente porque llegó a las Grandes Ligas apenas el 5 de abril de 2026 y rápidamente logró establecerse como uno de los receptores defensivos más destacados.
Durante su temporada de novato, Valenzuela disputó 91 encuentros con Toronto y se ubicó entre los cinco mejores receptores de MLB en métricas defensivas avanzadas.
De acuerdo con Statcast y FanGraphs, sus números fueron los siguientes:
- +11 carreras de valor defensivo (Fielding Run Value), según Statcast.
- +13.6 en calificación defensiva, de acuerdo con FanGraphs.
- +8 carreras mediante el enmarcado de lanzamientos, una habilidad que ayuda a convertir pitcheos cercanos a la zona en strikes.
- +5 carreras por sus tiros a las bases, reflejando su capacidad para controlar los intentos de robo.
- 19 corredores retirados en intento de robo, con una efectividad aproximada del 30.2%.
- 1.88 segundos de tiempo promedio de tiro a segunda base, desde la recepción de la pelota hasta su llegada a la almohadilla.
El mexicano también aportó ofensivamente, al registrar un promedio de bateo de .222, nueve cuadrangulares y 23 carreras impulsadas.
Su rendimiento le permitió formar una destacada dupla de receptores mexicanos con Alejandro Kirk, otro de los jugadores de Toronto reconocidos por su capacidad defensiva.
¿Quiénes compiten contra Brandon Valenzuela por el Guante de Oro?
El camino del hermosillense hacia el premio no será sencillo, pues deberá superar a dos receptores con números defensivos sobresalientes.
- Dillon Dingler (Tigres de Detroit): Es el actual ganador del Guante de Oro de la Liga Americana. Terminó la temporada con +17 en valor defensivo y una calificación defensiva de +22.1, liderando ambas métricas entre los receptores.
- Austin Wells (Yankees de Nueva York): Destacó por su capacidad para recibir lanzamientos y bloquear pelotas en la tierra. Registró +10 carreras de valor defensivo durante 2026.
- Brandon Valenzuela (Blue Jays de Toronto): Se colocó entre los mejores receptores defensivos pese a disputar menos encuentros que varios de sus competidores.
Dingler buscará conquistar su segundo Guante de Oro consecutivo, mientras que Valenzuela y Wells aspiran a obtener el primero de sus carreras.
¿En qué equipo de la LMP juega Brandon Valenzuela?
Aunque Brandon Valenzuela es originario de Hermosillo, Sonora, actualmente sus derechos en la Liga Mexicana del Pacífico (LMP) pertenecen a los Águilas de Mexicali, organización que lo adquirió mediante un intercambio con los Naranjeros de Hermosillo.
El movimiento se hizo oficial el 17 de junio de 2025, cuando los Naranjeros enviaron al receptor sonorense a Mexicali a cambio del infielder Milán Tolentino, hijo del exbeisbolista naranjero José Tolentino. El acuerdo fue de carácter definitivo entre ambas organizaciones.
Antes de su salida, Valenzuela había tenido actividad con los Naranjeros durante la temporada 2024-25, en la que disputó 28 encuentros, conectó 21 imparables, incluidos ocho extrabases, produjo 10 carreras y terminó con un promedio de bateo de .259.
El cambio se concretó cuando el catcher todavía pertenecía a la organización de los Padres de San Diego en el beisbol estadounidense. Posteriormente, el 31 de julio de 2025, pasó a los Blue Jays de Toronto en otro intercambio, esta vez a nivel de Grandes Ligas, por el infielder Will Wagner.
¿Quiénes son todos los finalistas al Guante de Oro 2026 de la Liga Americana?
Además de Brandon Valenzuela, entre los candidatos de la Liga Americana aparecen figuras como Bobby Witt Jr., Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Jacob deGrom y Cody Bellinger.

Los Blue Jays de Toronto encabezan la Liga Americana con cinco finalistas, incluyendo al hermosillense, Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Andrés Giménez, Nathan Lukes y José Soriano, quien también jugó para los Angelinos durante 2026.

En el Viejo Circuito, los Cachorros de Chicago también consiguieron cinco nominaciones, mientras que peloteros reconocidos como Chris Sale, Matt Olson, Dansby Swanson y Pete Crow-Armstrong buscarán sumar otro reconocimiento a sus trayectorias.

¿Cuándo se anunciarán los ganadores del Guante de Oro 2026 de MLB?
Los ganadores serán revelados el domingo 1 de noviembre de 2026, durante una edición especial de Baseball Tonight, transmitida por ESPN.
En las nueve posiciones tradicionales, los premios se determinan mediante dos componentes:
- 75%: Votación de los managers y entrenadores de Grandes Ligas, quienes no pueden seleccionar a jugadores de sus propios equipos.
- 25%: Índice Defensivo de la Sociedad para la Investigación del Beisbol Estadounidense (SABR), que utiliza estadísticas para evaluar el rendimiento defensivo.
La categoría de utility cuenta con una fórmula especializada desarrollada por Rawlings y SABR.
Posteriormente también se realizará la elección de los Guantes de Platino, que distinguen al mejor jugador defensivo de cada liga mediante una combinación de estadísticas y votaciones de los aficionados.
Para Brandon Valenzuela, la nominación representa una oportunidad de conquistar uno de los premios individuales más importantes de MLB en apenas su primera temporada, llevando el nombre de Hermosillo y Sonora a la élite defensiva del beisbol de Grandes Ligas.

Toronto Blue Jays veteran Kevin Pillar believes Alejandro Kirk's absence from the lineup contributed to Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s disappointing 2026 season, arguing that the first baseman struggled without reliable protection behind him.
Guerrero entered the season with high expectations after an impressive 2025 campaign, but he fell short of the offensive production many expected. Pillar believes the absence of Kirk, who signed a five-year, $58 million deal in 2025, forced Toronto to search for replacements who could provide the lineup support Guerrero needed. Kirk was absent from the Blue Jays' lineup from April to June after fracturing his left thumb. He sustained the injury on April 3 while catching a foul tip against the Chicago White Sox.
Speaking about the Blue Jays' offensive struggles, Pillar explained how the team struggled to find a consistent hitter to bat behind Guerrero. He also acknowledged that Guerrero had to take responsibility for his own performances and highlighted that the team struggled to find a reliable replacement, turning to players like Jesus Sanchez to fill the gap and provide the lineup protection Guerrero needed. Pillar said:
"But without Alejandro Kirk in the lineup, you know, they were looking for guys like Jesus Sanchez to step up. They were rotating some guys kind of in that spot to protect Vladdy. And obviously Vladdy didn't really help himself out this year by not having the type of year we think he's supposed to. But a big part of a guy like Vladdy having a good year is knowing he has someone behind him. And I think that got exposed this year when he went out of the lineup."
Vladimir Guerrero's struggles came in the first season of his 14-year, $500 million contract extension. The Blue Jays also endured a disappointing campaign, finishing with a 79-83 record and missing the playoffs.
He later faced criticism over comments about his contract during a Spanish-language interview with Dominican TV host Veronica Batista, prompting him to clarify his remarks to reporters in Baltimore in September.
What did Vladimir Guerrero Jr. say about his controversial remark on his contract and disappointing 2026 season?
During his conversation with reporters in Baltimore in September, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. explained that his comments had been taken out of context. He also expressed disappointment that he had been unable to help Toronto reach the postseason.
"That was a quote from the interview when she asked me how I felt about this year. I said that, obviously, I feel really bad about the year that I had, that I couldn't help my team get to the postseason. I said I felt, that it's my personal opinion, that every player gets paid for what they have done," said Guerrero.
He added:
"With that said, you guys have got to remember that I signed my contract at the beginning of last year, then I did put up a good year. Then, the kind of playoffs that I had to help the team get into the World Series."
Vladimir Guerrero finished the 2026 regular season with a .260 batting average, nine home runs and 57 RBIs across 144 games.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the calculus the Red Sox have to make when considering a potential contract extension for All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman. Be sure to join out FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
The Boston Red Sox made a massive gamble ahead of the trade deadline, sending a massive haul of prospects to the Baltimore Orioles in exchange for three-time All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman. After underperforming in 32 games with Boston, Rutschman now enters his final year of salary arbitration. But the Red Sox face a tough decision on whether to try to extend Rutschman ahead of the 2027 season.
Here's what a potential extension could look like:
What is Rutschman looking for?
Prior to being traded to Boston, Rutschman had exploratory talks with Baltimore about a potential extension. "Rutschman, then, would probably want a deal that makes him a lifetime Oriole, or close to it," wrote The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal on July 6. "His benchmark might be the nine-year, $167 million extension Buster Posey signed with the San Francisco Giants in March 2013," he continued.
The idea that Rutschman could be in line for a deal like Posey's, who will almost assuredly be in Cooperstown in the near future, is a bit far-fetched. Prior to signing that deal, Posey posted a career slash line of .314/.380/.503/.883 with 46 home runs and 191 RBI, winning the 2010 National League Rookie of the Year award, the 2012 National League Most Valuable Player award, and two World Series titles. A far cry from Rutschman's .252/.339/.414/.753 with 74 home runs and 290 RBI, with a career accolade list of three All-Star appearances.
Catchers typically struggle to capitalize on their value given the high injury risk from the wear and tear of being behind the plate nightly. Rutschman is no stranger to those concerns, having played just 189 games over the last two seasons.
Beyond Rutschman's worse resume than Posey's, the Red Sox have shied away from deals that take players well into their 30s, with the longest deal in recent memory being the eight-year extension given to Roman Anthony, which takes him through his age-29 season.
Comparisons
With Posey's nine-year deal seemingly out the window, we'll have to look at some more recent catcher deals, which… gets complicated, to say the least. Of the five richest deals signed by catchers, only one was signed with one year of service time remaining: Toronto Blue Jays' Alejandro Kirk. So let's start there:
Kirk
Ahead of the 2026 season, Kirk signed a five-year, $58-million deal to remain in Toronto through 2030. Before signing, Kirk was a two-time All-Star with a career line of .268/.345/.398/.743. Like Rutschman, Kirk is a strong defensive catcher when it comes to blocking balls in the dirt and framing. However, he struggles to throw runners out.
Though an average annual value of $11.6 million feels low based on Rosenthal's reporting, we'll have to keep looking.
Sean Murphy
At 29, Murphy signed a six-year, $73-million extension with the Atlanta Braves, buying out his final two years of arbitration. According to Spotrac, Murphy was paid $9 million in 2024, his penultimate arbitration year, and $15 million annually for the remainder of the deal.
At the time of signing, Murphy posted a .240/.336/.441/.778 line with 67 home runs and 215 RBI, earning an All-Star selection and becoming one of the game's best defensive catchers.
Cal Raleigh
The runner-up for the 2025 American League Most Valuable Player award, Raleigh signed a six-year, $105-million deal to remain with the Seattle Mariners through the 2030 season, buying out his final three arbitration years. In the four seasons leading up to his extension, Raleigh posted a line of .218/.296/.444/.740 with 93 home runs and 251 RBI. Defensively. Raleigh is a mixed bag, with improving blocking skills, but is middle of the road in both framing and throwing runners out.
Raleigh's deal is also slightly different than the one Rutschman would be looking to sign. While his deal carries an AAV of $17.5 million, the number is lower because he's receiving a lower salary in what would have been his arbitration years. Beginning in 2028, Raleigh will be paid $24.6 million annually.
Will Smith
Will Smith of the Los Angeles Dodgers has the richest catcher contract (by total value). Smith signed a 10-year, $140-million extension with Los Angeles ahead of the 2024 season, buying out his final two arbitration years. However, in typical Dodgers fashion, Smith will be paid $5 million annually from 2034-2043 in deferred payments, lowering the luxury tax hit to just $12 million annually. The deferred payments, expected to be a hot-button topic in ongoing labor talks, paired with Smith being paid through his age-38 season, make the comparison a bit far-fetched.
Before signing the deal, Smith hit .261/.357/.483/.840 with 91 home runs and 306 RBI over five seasons, while providing slightly above-average defense behind the plate.
So... Where does Rutschman fall?
Projecting contracts is an imperfect science. From a strictly production standpoint, Rutschman is most similar to Murphy or Kirk. However, neither player dealt with the same injury problems as Rutschman in the seasons leading up to their extensions. Murphy also represents the closest fit defensively to Rutschman, profiling as one of the best defensive catchers in the sport. The $15 million AAV Murphy would earn from 2025 through 2028 would seem to be the floor of what Rutschman would look for in a potential deal. With MLB Trade Rumors projecting Rutschman to make $9 million in arbitration in 2027, could the Red Sox bump that number up slightly to lower the value of the remainder of the deal to, say, $11 million in 2027 and $14-15 million each year after?
Then, of course, comes the term: catchers especially struggle to cash in on the open market later in their careers. Philadelphia Phillies backstop JT Realmuto posted a line of .257/.315/.384/.700 in 134 games in 2025 before hitting the open market ahead of his age-35 season. Realmuto sat on the free-agent market until Jan. 20, when he signed a three-year, $45-million extension to return to Philadelphia, a move widely criticized as an overpay for a catcher his age.
Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow will have to get creative to find common ground with Rutschman. A six-year contract would take him through his age-34 season, having him hit the market at a rather inopportune time. One possible solution for the Red Sox to give Rutschman the long-term commitment he's reportedly seeking could be to front-load the deal, paying him more in his prime while paying him incrementally less as he ages, reducing the franchise's financial burden as he ages and presumably declines.

item.content:encoded:
We’ve had some time for the dust to settle on the 2026 fantasy baseball season, which means it’s time to look back on what we learned (or should have learned) before we turn the page to 2027. I figured I’d start by looking at “league winners.”
We love to throw the term “league winner” around, but what does it really mean? I could have looked at all the teams who won leagues and found the players who appeared on most of them. That would be valid, but I don’t have all that data at my fingertips, and I believe the players who “won” you something were the players who outproduced their acquisition cost by the most. So that’s what I looked at: which players produced the most fantasy value based on what it cost to get them. Which players gave you the biggest return on investment. Chances are, if you hit on one or more of these guys, you were in for a pretty solid season.
To measure what their return on investment was, I took the FanGraphs Player Rater dollar values for 12-team leagues and used the Player Rater’s ADP, which is derived from NFBC formats. I compared what each player earned with what his draft position should have earned. The “should have earned” part, I needed some help with, so I had Claude average the 2026 earnings of every player drafted within a reasonable range (about 22%) of the ADP for that pick. So, for example, if the player was the 100th pick, I looked at the value produced by players drafted 78th through 128th. That felt like a fair way to say, “this pick should have produced a value around this amount.”
I referred to that below as their “Slot Cost.” Every pick after pick 250, I also treated as a waiver wire add, which meant it cost nothing to acquire the player. By taking the final dollar value for each player and subtracting their slot cost, we’re left with the players who earned far more than it cost to draft/acquire them.
So who were those players in 2026?
2026 Fantasy Baseball League-Winning Hitters
| Player | Pos | 2026 ADP | Slot cost | 2026 $ | Profit vs slot |
| Pete Crow-Armstrong | OF | 33 | $14.1 | $49.5 | +$35.5 |
| Jordan Walker | OF | 512 | $0.0 | $29.4 | +$29.4 |
| Ben Rice | C/1B/DH | 53 | $9.7 | $36.6 | +$26.9 |
| Miguel Vargas | 1B/3B | 303 | $0.0 | $26.5 | +$26.5 |
| Otto Lopez | 2B/SS | 229 | $0.0 | $26.5 | +$26.5 |
| CJ Abrams | SS | 65 | $9.1 | $33.9 | +$24.8 |
| Sal Stewart | 1B/3B | 162 | $3.3 | $27.9 | +$24.6 |
| Jake McCarthy | OF | 507 | $0.0 | $24.4 | +$24.4 |
| Gabriel Moreno | C/DH | 181 | $0.4 | $24.2 | +$23.8 |
| Alec Burleson | 1B/OF/DH | 175 | $0.9 | $23.9 | +$23.0 |
Not a ton of surprises here. Even though Pete Crow-Armstrong was a top 40 pick, he still vastly outperformed his draft slot. His production so far has exceeded everyone else’s, so he was the ultimate “league winner.” Ben Rice and CJ Abrams were also early-round picks who returned far more than it cost to acquire them, keeping in mind that Rice is catcher-eligible and this is for two-catcher formats.
PCA, Rice, and Abrams also join a group of hitters here who were already pretty good in 2025. Alec Burleson, Miguel Vargas, and Otto Lopez all had flashed usable production in 2025 and were locked into full-time roles. We may not have seen this jump coming, but we likely could have been drafting them higher based on underlying skills and roles.
We have talked ad nauseuam about Jordan Walker‘s breakout and ways in which we could have seen it coming. Sal Stewart was a highly touted rookie who delivered in his first full season, while both Gabriel Moreno and Jake McCarthy earned far more playing time than they were projected to. Moreno had never had more than 380 plate appearances in a season, but had 550 this year, and McCarthy won a starting job in Colorado, which also made him our staff vote for comeback player of the year.
Some other waiver wire players (ADP after pick 250) who came close to making this list were: Dillon Dingler ($22 value in 2026), Liam Hicks ($22), Jake Bauers ($20.8), Carter Jensen ($18.8), Luis Garcia Jr. ($18.6), Kevin McGonigle ($17.8), Carson Benge ($17.8), and Brooks Lee ($14.1).
2026 Fantasy Baseball League-Winning Pitchers
| Player | Pos | 2026 ADP | Slot cost | 2026 $ | Profit vs slot |
| Jacob Misiorowski | SP | 114 | $6.3 | $41.7 | +$35.4 |
| Cam Schlittler | SP | 117 | $5.2 | $37.6 | +$32.4 |
| Drew Rasmussen | SP | 132 | $4.9 | $28.9 | +$24.0 |
| Parker Messick | SP | 294 | $0.0 | $23.0 | +$23.0 |
| Jacob Latz | SP/RP | 731 | $0.0 | $17.6 | +$17.6 |
| Logan Henderson | SP | 413 | $0.0 | $17.4 | +$17.4 |
| Cade Cavalli | SP | 305 | $0.0 | $16.5 | +$16.5 |
| Nick Martinez | SP | 738 | $0.0 | $16.4 | +$16.4 |
| Dylan Cease | SP | 75 | $7.9 | $23.6 | +$15.7 |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | SP | 27 | $15.2 | $30.7 | +$15.6 |
Again, we start the list with names that are not particularly surprising. Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler were the best two pitchers in the league this season, and neither one of them was drafted inside the top 100 picks. Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Dylan Cease were the only two other semi-highly drafted pitchers who produced a “league-winning” return on your investment. I guess we can include Drew Rasmussen in there too.
Of this group of ten pitchers, five of them (Misiorowski, Schlittler, Logan Henderson, Parker Messick, and Cade Cavalli) were high strikeout rate arms who didn’t pitch enough innings in 2025 to be among the top arms drafted. In fairness to drafters, Parker Messick wasn’t officially in the rotation until the end of May, and Cade Cavalli was fairly mediocre until a pitch mix change and velocity bump in the middle of June. Still, betting on strikeout arms coming off limited workload makes sense.
The majority of the other names on here had a clear role/situation change. Drew Rasmussen was another year removed from injury and went up over 170 innings. Nick Martinez was given a chance to be a full-time starter, Jacob Latz was turned into a closer, and Dylan Cease changed organizations, which led to massive improvement from his changeup and attack plan.
So who could fit this bill in 2027?
Potential League-Winning Hitters in 2027
| Player | Pos | 2026 age | 2026 PA | Barrel % | 2026 $ |
| Heriberto Hernández | OF/DH | 26 | 505 | 12.7 | $4.1 |
| Spencer Torkelson | 1B | 26 | 612 | 12.2 | $6.0 |
| Colson Montgomery | 3B/SS | 24 | 638 | 12 | $7.6 |
| Munetaka Murakami | 1B | 26 | 553 | 20.5 | $9.1 |
| Chase DeLauter | OF/DH | 24 | 559 | 6.3 | $10.5 |
| Jac Caglianone | 1B/OF | 23 | 553 | 13 | $14.2 |
| Riley Greene | OF/DH | 25 | 592 | 14.8 | $14.6 |
| Garrett Mitchell | OF | 27 | 531 | 11.7 | $8.3 |
| Wilyer Abreu | OF | 27 | 681 | 12.5 | $13.2 |
| Luis García Jr. | 1B/2B | 26 | 543 | 12.2 | $18.6 |
If we’re going to identify who were league winners in 2026, then it makes sense to use that information to project who would be a league winner in 2027. The hitters who made the league winner list seemed to fall into two categories: Players who had already shown flashes of success and were underpriced (Rice, Burleson, Vargas, PCA, Lopez) and players who experienced a significant bump in playing time from the previous season (Walker, Stewart, McCarthy, Moreno).
It’s hard to use 2026 numbers to project who will have a playing time boost in 2027, so I’ll leave that part to the side for now. To find potentially underpriced hitters, I wanted to look at the commonalities behind the hitters who were “league winners” this year. Among all qualified hitters, having a 12%+ barrel rate or a 91+ mph average exit velocity, combined with being age 26 or younger, doubled the rate of $10+ profits returned. Meanwhile, strikeout rate, walk rate, chase rate, and swinging-strike rate had no relationship to profit.
That means, if we’re looking for players to break out in 2027, we should be looking for players entering their athletic prime who hit the ball hard. Not a shocking revelation, and I already write an off-season column about hitters entering their athletic prime years. This year, that column mentioned Rice, Vargas, Lopez, Ryan Jeffers, Wilyer Abreu, Alejandro Kirk, and a collection of hitters who did not break out (Brett Baty, Heliot Ramos, Andrew Vaughn, etc.)
In addition to the list above, there are a few players who fit the hard contact and age profile but will likely already be priced up by the market. I’m not going to list them as potential league winners, but they should be targets for you in drafts, even at cost: Walker, Stewart, Vargas, Drake Baldwin, Hunter Goodman, Carter Jensen, James Wood and Jackson Chourio. All earned $18–30 this season and could see a sizeable boost from that in 2027.
Of the others listed, Jac Caglianone might be the best fit based on age and his 13% barrel rate and 93.3 mph average exit velocity. We already know why Riley Greene is an exciting fantasy option, but he produced just $15 of value in 2026. There’s a path for him to be a $30+ guy. Heriberto Hernandez and Chase DeLauter could take big steps forward with more playing time; Luis Garcia Jr. has a full season in Yankee Stadium, and all of Spencer Torkelson, Munetaka Murakami, and Colson Montgomery have the batted ball quality but major contact issues. If they can make strides in their contact rates, their power could lead to a massive return on investment for fantasy.
Potential League-Winning Pitchers in 2027
| Player | Team | Pos | 2026 IP | K/IP | 2026 $ |
| Didier Fuentes | ATL | SP/RP | 73.1 | 1.26 | $9.1 |
| Jonah Tong | NYM | SP | 30.2 | 1.13 | -$3.6 |
| Tatsuya Imai | HOU | SP | 76.2 | 1.27 | -$7.3 |
| Gage Jump | ATH | SP | 98.2 | 1.10 | -$15.4 |
| Brandon Sproat | MIL | SP | 97.0 | 1.04 | -$16.3 |
| Jack Leiter | TEX | SP | 80.0 | 1.04 | -$12.8 |
| Jackson Jobe | DET | SP | 46.0 | 1.11 | -$2.1 |
| Mason Montgomery | PIT | SP/RP | 68.2 | 1.54 | $13.3 |
| Grant Taylor | CHW | SP/RP | 84.0 | 1.26 | $13.8 |
Looking at the starting pitchers who made our “league-winners” list earlier in the article, the key is strikeouts. Among all starters drafted at an ADP between 90–400, those who threw under 100 innings in 2025 and posted a 1.0 K/IP or higher averaged $4.40 or more when compared to their slot, and 31% of them returned $10+ profit. So we need to be looking for starting pitchers like that. The names that came up were Didier Fuentes, Jonah Tong, and Logan Henderson. Of course, Henderson already was a “league-winner” in 2026, so his price will be high.
Younger pitchers who had the strikeouts but a poor ERA also fit the bill. Remember that Misiorowski had a 4.36 ERA in 2025. He was missing tons of bats, but the surface-level ratios weren’t ideal. Pitchers like Tatsuya Imai, Brandon Sproat, Jackson Jobe, and Jack Leiter all fit the bill. So did Gage Jump and Mason Barnett, but factoring in the element of pitching in Sacramento muddies those waters.
The other names on this list, Mason Montgomery and Grant Taylor, are either elite closers or potentially breakout starters if they’re moved back into the rotation. There is obviously a lot of uncertainty with their roles in 2027, but they are names to keep an eye on, especially if we have a better idea of their role.

La trayectoria de Jonathan Aranda representa un recorrido destacado desde el beisbol infantil de Tijuana hasta los escenarios más importantes de las Grandes Ligas. El tijuanense pasó de formarse en los campos de la Liga Municipal de Tijuana a convertirse en pieza fundamental de los Tampa Bay Rays, equipo que aseguró su lugar en las Series Divisionales de los Playoffs de la MLB.
Durante la temporada regular 2026, Aranda tuvo un papel protagonista dentro de la ofensiva de Tampa Bay. El primera base e infielder mostró consistencia con el bate y terminó la campaña con un promedio de .277, además de sumar 156 imparables, 22 cuadrangulares y 92 carreras producidas, cifras que reflejan su importancia en el orden ofensivo de los Rays.
Su rendimiento fue determinante para que Tampa Bay alcanzara los playoffs con la mira puesta en avanzar a las siguientes rondas. Para Aranda, la clasificación representa otro paso importante en una carrera que comenzó en el beisbol tijuanense y que ahora lo coloca frente a uno de los mayores retos de su trayectoria. Aquí en Heraldo Deportes te contamos sus inicios y cómo llegó a Grandes Ligas.
Así fueron los humildes inicios de Jonathan Aranda en el beisbol de Tijuana
Jonathan Aranda encontró en el béisbol una oportunidad para mantenerse alejado de los entornos de violencia en Tijuana y construir un camino ligado al deporte. Nacido el 23 de mayo de 1998 en Baja California, comenzó a jugar desde pequeño con el respaldo de sus padres, Humberto Aranda y Ventura, quienes veían en esta actividad una forma de fomentar la disciplina y mantenerlo protegido. Con el paso de los años, aquella iniciativa familiar se convirtió en el inicio de una carrera que lo llevaría hasta las Grandes Ligas.
Durante su infancia, Aranda desarrolló su talento en las ligas infantiles y juveniles de Tijuana, donde destacó especialmente en la Liga Municipal. En esos campos también forjó una amistad con Alejandro Kirk, otro pelotero tijuanense que alcanzaría el máximo nivel del béisbol profesional. Ambos compartieron sus primeros pasos en el diamante y, con el tiempo, transformaron aquellos años de formación en una trayectoria que los llevaría a representar a México en la MLB.
Te puede interesar: Playoffs MLB 2026: Así puedes VER EN VIVO los juegos entre Yankees y Red Sox de Grandes Ligas
La historia de cómo Jonathan Aranda llegó a Grandes Ligas
El camino profesional de Jonathan Aranda comenzó con los Toros de Tijuana, donde fue identificado como uno de los jóvenes talentos de la región. El tijuanense pasó cerca de dos años dentro del sistema de desarrollo del club, trabajando principalmente en su capacidad de contacto y preparación ofensiva. En 2016 tuvo actividad con los Toros de Moroleón en la Liga Invernal Mexicana, una etapa que le permitió adquirir experiencia y llamar la atención de organizaciones de Grandes Ligas.
Su oportunidad con los Tampa Bay Rays surgió durante una sesión de visoría realizada en Tijuana en 2015. Los cazatalentos habían acudido para observar a Randy Arozarena, quien entrenaba con los Toros, y terminaron siguiendo de cerca el desempeño de Aranda. El bateador tijuanense convenció por su técnica y capacidad ofensiva, por lo que los Rays decidieron firmarlo por un bono de 130 mil dólares, dando inicio a su recorrido por las ligas menores. Siete años después, en 2022, Aranda debutó en la MLB y comenzó una nueva etapa de su carrera en el máximo nivel del béisbol.

The Toronto Blue Jays entered 2026 expecting their offence to help carry them to another postseason run. Instead, a lineup that had been central to the club’s World Series appearance a year earlier became one of its biggest weaknesses. Established stars endured dramatic downturns, useful role players were asked to carry larger workloads and injuries forced Toronto to lean on several inexperienced hitters.
Anyone who watched the Blue Jays in 2026 knows they were not a good offensive team. They scored the fewest runs in all of baseball (648), hit the fewest home runs (152), and ranked second-worst in team OPS (.691) ahead of only the Los Angeles Angels.
There were still a few encouraging performances. But for every one of those successes they Blue Jays had another two or three hitters who fell short of expectations. The grades below weigh each hitter’s production against his role, opportunity and expectations entering the season.
Grading every Blue Jays hitter from the 2026 season
Alejandro Kirk
- HR: 10
- RBI: 43
- AVG: .278
- OPS: .767
- wRC+: 114
Kirk didn’t look like himself to start the year, then missed several months with a thumb injury. He recaptured his All-Star form when he finally returned, however, and led the Blue Jays offensively for much of the second half.
Grade: B+
Andrés Giménez
- HR: 9
- RBI: 59
- AVG: .244
- OPS: .649
- wRC+: 81
Giménez is what he is at this point: a below-average hitter with a knack for coming through in the clutch. He still managed to accrue 2.8 fWAR on the strength of his stellar glovework at shortstop and contributions on the basepaths.
Grade: B-
Brandon Valenzuela
- HR: 9
- RBI: 24
- AVG: .226
- OPS: .688
- wRC+: 96
Valenzuela filled in admirably for Kirk while he was on the injured list during the first half of the season. He flashed legitimate power upside at the plate before going ice-cold after the All-Star break, exposing the current limitations of his offensive profile.
Grade: C
Brett Bateman
- HR: 2
- RBI: 11
- AVG: .329
- OPS: .826
- wRC+: 138
Bateman exceeded all expectations after being acquired for Kevin Gausman at the trade deadline. He injected some life into the lineup immediately upon arrival and has likely cemented himself as a marquee piece of the 2027 squad.
Grade: A+
Charles McAdoo
- HR: 3
- RBI: 14
- AVG: .258
- OPS: .694
- wRC+: 93
McAdoo largely held his own at the plate with the Blue Jays in 2026. His approach needs work, but his combination of power and speed is exciting. He should keep improving with additional reps against MLB pitching.
Grade: C+
Davis Schneider
- HR: 5
- RBI: 16
- AVG: .145
- OPS: .624
- wRC+: 84

As you can see from the Blue Jays announcement, Alejandro Kirk has been replaced by Valenzuela for Sunday’s final game. It will be the 25-year-old‘s 91st game of the year.
Additionally, George Springer, Charles McAdoo, Davis Schneider, and Myles Straw are also coming into the lineup. Coming out in their place are Nathan Lukes, Sean Keys, and Josh Smith.
Looking At Brandon Valenzuela & Alejandro Kirk
Valenzuela has been a solid contributor for the Blue Jays this season.
The young catcher has recorded 53 hits, 22 RBIs, two stolen bases, nine doubles, 28 walks, and eight home runs in 90 games. He started 83 games at catcher and five games at first base.
On the other hand, Kirk has been one of the bright spots of the Blue Jays’ otherwise down year.
In 79 games, the 27-year-old recorded 77 hits, eight doubles, 43 RBIs, one stolen base, 33 walks, and 10 home runs.

Valenzuela’s future with the Blue Jays is uncertain.
However, if Springer moves on from Toronto, there will be room for Valenzuela. Kirk has been a better hitter than Valenzuela, making him an easy choice to slide into the designated hitter role. However, if Valenzuela improves his swing, he could spend some games at DH, too.

One way or another, Valenzuela will be an active member of the Blue Jays for at least another year.

Las Grandes Ligas comienzan a llegar a su fin. Con octubre a la vuelta de la esquina, los equipos de la MLB arrancan el camino rumbo al sueño de la Serie Mundial, desafortunadamente, para algunos equipos significa el fin del camino, caso de ello el de los Toronto Blue Jays, quienes sorpresivamente quedaron fuera de los Playoffs de la Liga Americana.
Referentes de México fuera
Pese a ser uno de los mejores equipos el año pasado, los Azulejos de Toronto no lograron encontrar el ritmo durante la temporada, dejando una marca de 77-81 y quedando matemáticamente eliminado de su zona.
La novena que cuenta con mexicanos como referentes, tales como: Alejandro Kirk, Brandon Valenzuela y José Rodríguez, quedó fuera oficialmente luego de caer ante los Orioles en su Juego 3 y siendo barridos en la serie.
Toronto llegó a este tramo de la temporada con pocas posibilidades de mantenerse con vida en la pelea por un boleto a la Postemporada. La novena canadiense no logró repetir el protagonismo que tuvo durante la campaña anterior y terminó alejándose de los puestos que daban acceso a octubre.
Para los mexicanos, la eliminación significa también el final de su participación en la campaña. Alejandro Kirk volvió a ser una de las piezas mexicanas más reconocidas dentro de la organización, aunque sufrió una importante lesión a mitad de campaña, mientras que Brandon Valenzuela y José Rodríguez fueron poco más frecuentes.
De la Serie Mundial a quedar fuera
El contraste es importante para los Blue Jays, pues después de disputar la Serie Mundial en 2025, el equipo no consiguió mantenerse en la pelea por el campeonato durante esta temporada. La novena canadiense perdió terreno conforme avanzó el calendario y terminó sin posibilidades de regresar a la lucha por el título.
Ahora, Kirk, Valenzuela y Rodríguez deberán esperar al próximo año para volver a buscar un lugar en la Postemporada de las Grandes Ligas. Mientras tanto, Toronto tendrá que comenzar a planear una temporada baja en la que buscará recuperar el nivel mostrado el año pasado.

The Toronto Blue Jays are looking to avoid being swept by the Texas Rangers on Sunday and have made some changes to their lineup.

The Blue Jays are now 76-79.
Toronto Blue Jays Announce Brandon Valenzuela News
Toronto is looking to avoid the series sweep and has made some major changes to its lineup.
The Blue Jays are resting some regular players, as starting catcher Alejandro Kirk is getting the day off, with Brandon Valenzuela getting the start. He will also be hitting eighth.

Toronto will start Spencer Miles as the opener, as it's a bullpen game with Spencer Arrighetti getting the bulk of the innings.
Kirk getting the day off isn't a surprise, as Valenzuela has been catching and starting a lot on Sunday to give Kirk the day off in the series finale.
Valenzuela is a great defensive catcher with a cannon of an arm, yet his bat has struggled as of late. He's hitting .217 with 8 home runs and 21 RBIs. However, in his last 7 games, he's hitting .105 with 0 home runs and 0 RBIs, while striking out 5 times.
Toronto Right Now

Toronto lost the first two games of a three-game road series against Texas, which seemingly ended their playoff hopes. The Blue Jays have been blown out in both of their games against the Rangers, which is frustrating for the team.
Jose Soriano struggled in the outing, which was frustrating for the team as the Blue Jays sent Dylan Cease and Soriano, their two best pitchers, in the first two games.
"We're still positive. Doesn't matter the result, we're still positive," said Soriano. "We're not going to win every game we play. The other team's trying to win, too. So, we try to control what we can control and play one game at a time."

¿Qué mexicanos ya tienen encaminado su boleto?
Entre los jugadores que tienen su lugar asegurado destaca Jonathan Aranda, infielder tijuanense de los Tampa Bay Rays, franquicia que matemáticamente consiguió su clasificación a la postemporada y que se mantiene en la parte alta de la División Este de la Liga Americana.
Otro nombre que se encuentra en plena pelea es Jarren Durán, jardinero mexicoamericano de los Boston Red Sox. El pelotero forma parte de una novena que pelea por mantenerse en la zona de clasificación del joven circuito y que apunta a disputar la Serie de Comodines si consigue sostener su posición.
Por su parte, Alejandro Kirk continúa siendo una de las principales referencias mexicanas en las Grandes Ligas. El receptor de los Toronto Blue Jays afronta con su equipo una cerrada lucha por ingresar a los Playoffs de la Liga Americana, con cada partido de la recta final teniendo un peso importante en sus aspiraciones.
La pelea también está en la Liga Nacional
En el Viejo Circuito también hay varios peloteros con posibilidades de disputar la postemporada. Alek Thomas, jardinero mexicoamericano de los Arizona Diamondbacks, se encuentra involucrado en la cerrada pelea por los últimos boletos de comodín de la Liga Nacional.
Los San Diego Padres también cuentan con representación mexicana con Jeremiah Estrada, relevista mexicoamericano que forma parte del bullpen de una organización que se mantiene en puestos que actualmente entregarían un boleto a la postemporada mediante el comodín.
Mientras tanto, Javier Assad vive una situación favorable con los Chicago Cubs. El pitcher tijuanense forma parte de una novena que tiene prácticamente encaminada su clasificación, con los Cachorros ubicados en una posición privilegiada dentro de la carrera por los Playoffs de la Liga Nacional.
Otros jugadores también permanecen atentos a la definición de la temporada. Taijuan Walker, con los Philadelphia Phillies, así como JoJo Romero y Ramón Urías, con los St. Louis Cardinals, buscan mantener a sus respectivos equipos dentro de la conversación por los últimos lugares disponibles en la Nacional.
